item.title: BOBBY BURACK: The anti-white resistance is already beginning for Cooper Flagg
item.description: Cooper Flagg's rise as a 19-year-old Dallas Mavericks star is sparking a heated racial debate after ex-NBA player Charlie Villanueva's comments.
item.content:encoded:
Dallas Mavericks forward Cooper Flagg is 19 years old and already one of the best basketball players in the world.

Last week, ESPN analyst Jeremy Lin called him "generational" and said he and Victor Wembanyama could become the NBA’s next great rivalry.

Flagg has also drawn favorable comparisons to LeBron James at the same age, including from Brian Windhorst.

"In my view, Cooper is better at defense than LeBron was at the same age. I don’t even think it’s debatable," Windhorst said.

"There were defensive plays LeBron made at that age. He certainly would get into passing lanes, he certainly would block shots, he was a defensive playmaker, but Cooper is better defensively, empirically; I don’t think that’s debatable."

CARTON MOCKS KANSAS CITY CHIEFS AFTER HEARTBREAKING WEEK 8 LOSS - DOWNLOAD NOW

Flagg is averaging 27 points, six rebounds and seven assists during his second season.

A phenom of Flagg’s caliber should be a gift to the NBA as some of its biggest stars, including LeBron James, Steph Curry and Kevin Durant, approach the end of their careers. Instead, his rise may expose the worst instincts in sports.

Cooper Flagg is White. For some members of the basketball community, that is a problem. Former NBA player Charlie Villanueva is one of them.

Villanueva discussed Flagg’s rising stardom on the "To The Baha" podcast last week. According to Villanueva, Flagg cannot become the face of the NBA because of his skin color.

"This might sound crazy, but I don’t think in 2026 a White dude could be, I’m gonna be real, could be the face of the league, if I’m being honest," Villanueva said. "Because it’s a Black league, right?"

EMBRACE OF WEMBY AS FACE OF THE NBA PROVES RESISTANCE TOWARD JOKIC WAS ALWAYS RACIAL | BOBBY BURACK

He then argued that a White player cannot become the best player in the NBA.

"When is the last time we’ve seen a White man be the face of the league? Don’t say Larry Bird, they had to pair him up with Magic," Villanueva said. "When was the last time a White man was single-handedly the best player in the league?"

That talking point was predictable. OutKick predicted it days after Flagg became the first overall pick out of Duke last season.

DAKICH: SPORTS MEDIA HAS CREATED AN ‘INDUSTRY’ OUT OF COMPLAINING ABOUT WHITE ATHLETES LIKE CAITLIN CLARK

For the past three to four years, several former Black players comfortably expressed belittling views of White players.

The hysteria surrounding Caitlin Clark began with the claim that her popularity and stardom resulted from "White privilege." Black players have called Luka Doncic a "bitch ass white boy" on the court. ESPN analyst Kendrick Perkins falsely accused NBA MVP voters of favoring Nikola Jokic because he is white, likely costing him the award in 2023.

More recently, Stephen A. Smith claimed a team could not win a championship built around white players. Former broadcaster Mark Jones has posted several bigoted messages about Jokic. Gilbert Arenas has joked about exiling white players from the league.

ESPN has published several articles framing Jokic, Clark, and Doncic as "great white hopes," despite the evidence to the contrary.

The pattern is obvious. Anti-white bigotry has become accepted and, at times, rewarded in public discourse. It has been normalized since 2020.

Notice Villanueva’s wording: The NBA is "a Black league, right?"

STEPHEN A SMITH SHOWS HIS PRIVILEGE BY MOCKING LAKERS' ROSTER FOR HAVING TOO MANY 'WHITE DUDES'

That view echoes comments from Arenas and others who refer to the NBA as "our" league. These Black players appear territorial about the sport and seem threatened when white players succeed.

For context, consider what activist and social media influencer Dr. Umar Johnson said about Eminem in 2023. Johnson claimed Eminem should be excluded from the conversation about the greatest rappers of all time because of his skin color.

"No non-African can ever be the best of anything African. It’s an insult to the ancestors. It’s an insult to the race and it’s an insult to every black person."

Johnson then claimed the black community should never have allowed Eminem into hip-hop.

"Eminem has all the privileges of a white male and all the privileges of being in the hip hop community, so we got to be careful about letting non-Africans into our community."

That is the message Black players send about White basketball players: Basketball is their sport. White people are merely their guests.

Of course, the premise is illogical. Basketball is not a black space. A White man created it. No sport or musical genre belongs to any race in America.

The popularity of both White and Black athletes and entertainers makes that clear. Normal Americans like Eminem for the same reasons they like Tupac, Biggie, or Jay Z. They like Jokic, Clark, Doncic, and Flagg for the same reasons they like LeBron James, Michael Jordan, and Kobe Bryant.

Unfortunately, people with the largest platforms too often promote an isolated worldview in which race determines who deserves admiration, legitimacy, and power.

Flagg could prove particularly polarizing.

The usual suspects tried dismissing Jokic and Doncic as international players. Flagg does not give them that option. He was born in Maine. He attended Duke.

His charismatic personality also gives him marketing potential that Jokic and Doncic lacked.

If Flagg emerges as a true face of the post-LeBron NBA, expect the race idolaters to react accordingly. They will resist him and diminish him with the usual racial buzzwords. They will cast his supporters as racists and sellouts.

Sound familiar?

Of course, it does. It's the response every great white basketball player now receives.

For Flagg, Villanueva's comments were just the beginning.

item.title: JACKSON THOMPSON: Maine girls speak out about facing trans athlete as state grapples with issue
item.description: Two Maine high school girls describe "crushing disappointment" competing against transgender athletes as their attorney files a Title IX complaint.
item.content:encoded:
Two Maine high school girls spoke out Monday about competing against transgender athletes, describing "crushing disappointment" and urging officials to protect their opportunities as their attorney announced plans for a federal civil rights complaint.

Reagan Wilson, a junior at Fryeburg Academy, and Morgan Clark, a junior and varsity soccer captain at Windham High School, addressed a news conference at the Maine State House in Augusta alongside advocates seeking a statewide vote on sex-based eligibility rules.

"Many girls and women are discovering the crushing disappointment that comes from being beaten in their own sports by males who should have never been allowed to compete in the first place," Wilson said.

TRANSGENDER ATHLETES HAVE TAKEN 2,293 CHAMPIONSHIP SPOTS FROM BIOLOGICAL WOMEN, NEW RESEARCH FINDS

Wilson, who said she has competed in swimming, cross-country, indoor and outdoor track, soccer and softball, described facing transgender competitors across multiple seasons.

"During my cross-country season, I competed against a biological male in many of my races. Most recently, I competed against a male playing on an all-girls soccer team," she said.

"This is unacceptable and has deprived me and so many other girls of equal opportunity to compete and win."

Clark, who said she has played soccer in Maine since she was 4, described the issue moving from something she encountered online to something affecting her own team.

COLORADO SCHOOL PARENTS SOUND ALARM AFTER DAUGHTERS WERE CUT FROM VOLLEYBALL TEAM WHILE TRANS ATHLETE PLAYS

"Last year, this sort of thing was something I only saw online, but now it’s something that I’m seeing in my own field," Clark said. "If it can happen to me, it can happen to you."

Clark pointed to an October tie against a team whose results had improved substantially over the previous season.

"In October, our team tied against a team we’ve easily outranked in past years, a team with a male athlete," she said.

Windham played South Portland to a 1-1 draw on Oct. 1. The Portland Press Herald reported that South Portland finished the previous season 3-9-2 and 14th in the regional Heal point standings.

A draft complaint provided to OutKick identifies a transgender player on South Portland’s girls’ soccer team as the focus of the athletes’ allegations. A scoring chart supplied for the planned complaint credited the player with 15 goals and 10 assists through South Portland’s Oct. 27 playoff game.

The draft alleges that Maine’s eligibility policies deprive female athletes of equal competitive opportunities. It also describes Wilson’s previous experiences in cross-country and indoor track and field.

CARTON MOCKS KANSAS CITY CHIEFS AFTER HEARTBREAKING WEEK 8 LOSS - DOWNLOAD NOW

At Monday’s news conference, Alliance Defending Freedom attorney Tavia Bruxellas McAlister said the organization would file a Title IX complaint that day on the girls’ behalf with the U.S. Department of Education’s Office for Civil Rights.

The draft seeks an investigation of the Maine Department of Education, Maine Principals’ Association, South Portland School Department and Windham Raymond School District, along with changes to eligibility policies and remedies for alleged past violations.

Both Windham and South Portland were eliminated in regional semifinals Friday, ending the possibility of another meeting during this year’s playoffs. The draft says both girls intend to play varsity soccer again next year and expect to face the South Portland athlete.

Maine’s policy dispute with the federal government predates the girls’ planned complaint. The Education Department announced a Title IX noncompliance finding against Maine in March 2025, and the Justice Department sued the state’s education department the following month over transgender participation in girls’ sports.

Maine officials and the MPA have defended their approach by citing the Maine Human Rights Act, which protects against gender-identity discrimination. The MPA’s published policy allows transgender students to compete according to either their birth sex or gender identity, but not both.

In June, the Supreme Court upheld state restrictions on transgender participation in girls’ and women’s sports. The Court expressly left unresolved whether schools may allow transgender athletes to participate on female teams, the separate question underlying Maine’s dispute.

The athletes appeared as referendum organizers announced another attempt to put restrictions before Maine voters.

Leyland Streiff, principal officer of the Protect Girls Sports in Maine ballot committee and a leader of Maine Girl Dads, said the group was submitting 4,836 additional signatures toward a place on the 2027 ballot.

Its earlier petition fell 532 valid signatures short of qualifying for this year’s election after a legal challenge and review. Additional signatures would require state validation.

The proposal would base eligibility for designated school teams and access to bathrooms, locker rooms and other private spaces on sex recorded on students’ original birth certificates. It would also allow students to sue over qualifying violations.

Clark said she hopes the effort changes the experience for her teammates and other girls.

"I hope that this referendum helps girls like me and my friends play the sport that we love fairly and safely," she said.

item.title: Actor Bill Murray stuns Trump's top economic advisor with bizarre question on news show
item.description: Bill Murray asked Kevin Hassett to say "my dog just died" on CNBC's "Squawk Box" to test his ever-present smile during a live interview moment Monday.
item.content:encoded:
Actor Bill Murray posed an unusual question to National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett during an appearance on CNBC's "Squawk Box" Monday morning.

The "Ghostbusters" and "Groundhog Day" actor was on CNBC to promote his new six-part travel and golf docuseries "A Course Called Ireland," which premiered last week. Later in the program, Murray was invited by "Squawk Box" host Joe Kernen to ask Hassett a question.

WHITE HOUSE ECONOMIST PROJECTS GDP GROWTH COULD TOP 5% AMID CAPITAL SPENDING BOOM

While continuing to smile, Hassett asked, "Oh, well, is it your dog or my dog?"

"Your dog," Murray answered.

"We were gonna have someone go take your blood. We’re gonna call them off. Not gonna happen," Murray remarked.

BILL MURRAY IS THE ULTIMATE SPORTS DAD AS SON LUKE LEADS UCONN TO FINAL FOUR AFTER DEFEATING DUKE
